Essay in a Dialectical Introduction to Philosophy
based on Hegel’s Phenomenology as interpreted in the light of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism

The manuscript published here in two volumes under the general title Sophia is almost as enigmatic as Kojève’s life itself (1902–1968). We know virtually nothing about the history of the text. It remains unpublished in Russian, though the V–A–C Foundation is preparing an edition under the direction of Karen Sarkissov. Its story is therefore mysterious—and, from the little we do know, at times almost unbelievable.

The manuscript itself tells us that Kojève intended it to be “printed in the USSR” and “accepted as a doctoral dissertation” after passing “sociopolitical and cultural ‘censorship.’” It also tells us that he worked on it for more than six months, from 28 November 1940 to 9 June 1941. Beyond that, almost everything is hypothetical, though some of the hypotheses have a certain charm.
A. Rutkevič, the Russian Kojève specialist, writes in his preface to an extract from the work:

Kojève was living in his small apartment outside Paris, and over the course of half a year he wrote nearly 1,000 pages. Nina Ivanoff [Kojève’s second partner] once told me that in May 1941 he went with L. Poliakov—the future historian of antisemitism—to the Soviet embassy to deliver his manuscript. More plausibly, what he brought there would have been a typescript of part of the text he was then working on, but this is only a hypothesis. It could just as easily have been an entirely different document. It is even possible that none of this happened at all, since Nina Ivanoff is our only source and she herself spoke of it tentatively. When I asked her directly whether Kojève had had a text typed at that time, she said no. And when I asked whether he had given it to a typist, she expressed serious doubts. In any case, on 22 June 1941, before the embassy was evacuated, most of the papers kept there were burned. That is why we have no way of knowing exactly what had been taken there. As for the fantasies of “postmodern” prose writers who claim that this was some kind of “letter to Stalin,” we can leave that to their consciences. Once the manuscript was finished, Kojève gave it to Bataille before leaving Paris. He moved to the south of France, in the Free Zone. Then, from 1942 onward, he became a member of the Resistance.

Rutkevič is right that the manuscript is certainly not a “letter to Stalin” in any formal sense. Even so, we cannot simply dismiss that hypothesis as something invented by Anglo-American “postmodern writers.” Rubin, Kojève’s friend, advances it with some confidence in his Russian biography of him. More importantly, it fits, at least to some degree, with Kojève’s openly stated ambitions: to become “Stalin’s consciousness,” to achieve philosophical success in the USSR, and to obtain a political role there.

The manuscript’s accidental rediscovery is just as remarkable. It had apparently been kept in the same safe as a manuscript by Walter Benjamin, while the typescript may have been burned when the Soviet embassy in Paris was evacuated. Jocelyn Monchamp, curator at the BnF responsible for the “Kojève collection,” briefly reconstructs the story on the BnF website:

The history of the manuscript is unusual compared with the rest of Kojève’s archive. In 1941, the author entrusted it to Georges Bataille, who was then a librarian in the Periodicals Department of the Bibliothèque nationale. Before crossing the demarcation line and settling in Provence, Kojève asked his friend to put the text somewhere safe. Kojève himself kept only the preparatory file for the work, which contained projected plans for its various sections, together with the final sheet of the part he had written—probably because he intended to resume work on it later. These documents remained among Kojève’s papers and were donated to the BnF, along with the rest of his working manuscripts, by his partner Nina Ivanoff in 2001. The manuscript entrusted to Bataille remained at the Bibliothèque nationale until Bataille’s death in 1962. It was found in his office in 1963 and passed by Jean Prinet, chief curator of the Periodicals Department, to the General Administrator, who transferred it to the Manuscripts Department in July 1963. It was not entered into the inventory until 1992, under the donation number “D. 92-24,” and was later reunited with the rest of Kojève’s papers after the Ivanoff donation arrived.
The “Phenomenological Autobiography” of a Soviet Kojève
This mysterious text, which Kojève would never mention again after the war, is nevertheless central to understanding his work.

In 2003, opening a study day devoted to Kojève, Florence de Lussy argued perceptively that anyone who wanted to understand the “Kojève case” needed this manuscript as one of the essential keys. She was right. But it took another twenty years for that judgment to be confirmed—for the manuscript to be transcribed and translated, and for readers finally to gain access to this missing key, perhaps even to Kojève’s masterpiece.

The mystery surrounding the Kojève “case” may now begin to clear. Laurent Jeanpierre seems to sense as much when he writes in an article for Critique that “in the end, Kojève remains a mystery, perhaps because no one has yet reconstructed his life and work together.” A key was missing. We now possess it. His postwar role as a “philosopher-adviser” to major “decision-makers” must be reconsidered in light of a manuscript that has remained entirely unpublished until now: an unfinished manuscript begun in November 1940 and broken off in the summer of 1941, when Kojève moved to the southern zone. It shows that we should take literally what he told Tran-Duc-Thao in 1948: that his lectures on Hegel “were essentially a work of propaganda designed to make an impact on people’s minds.” The manuscript, written in Russian under the title Sofia – Filosofia i Fenomeno-logia, survives together with a detailed plan revealing the full scope of the intended work. It is the work of a militant. Through Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit, it develops a “discourse” interpreted resolutely along Marxist-Leninist lines.

But the manuscript is more than a simple “missing link in the life and work of the enigmatic Kojève.” Above all, it is an original work in which Kojève finally speaks in his own name. He even promises to recount his own “autobiography.”

Yet when he presents the book as an act of coming to self-awareness, or as a “phenomenological autobiography,” we must immediately add that this is not the self-awareness of an isolated individual. It is also the self-awareness of an entire people—Russia—as it confronts universal history.
Or, more precisely, if this really is the self-awareness of an individual, we must remember that for Kojève the individual is always a microcosm containing the whole of History.
So if this is an “autobiography,” it is an autobiography on the scale of Russia itself: a vast country seeking to transform the world.
It is difficult to know why Kojève abandoned the work unfinished when he had already drawn up plans for a project of far greater scope. But his intention is clear. He wants to “justify” the USSR.
For the “Soviet” philosopher, however, to “justify” the USSR means more than explaining it or showing dialectically how it emerged from the past. It also means helping to bring it to completion.

Kojève wants to take part in the realization of this new Empire. As he put it near the beginning of his career, he wants to help prepare “the construction of a new culture” by bringing himself “into step with his time,” which for him means taking the side of the Russian Revolution.

The book before us is therefore Kojève’s contribution to the “construction of this new culture”: a Soviet culture that was supposed to fulfill the messianic aspirations of the Russian peoples and bring world history to completion.
What Kojève proposes here thus has the character of a Soviet citizen’s duty:

The duty of every person who sees communist society as their ideal is to devote all their strength to achieving that goal. The goal may be logically necessary, but it becomes factually possible only through conscious and active effort.
Kojève therefore wanted to participate in the realization of history itself, which was supposed to culminate in communism—or in a World Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.

Did he really hope, as has sometimes been claimed, to convince Stalin himself and thereby earn the right to participate politically in Soviet affairs? It is not impossible. But establishing this would require further biographical research, especially into Kojève’s extensive correspondence.
A Work of “Propaganda” Behind the Mask of Hegel
For now, Kojève remains, in Marco Filoni’s apt phrase, “an unrecognized classic.”

A “classic,” certainly, because of his interpretation of Hegel and especially of the “master-slave dialectic”: the “struggle for recognition” that Kojève presents as the true birth of humanity and history.
What remains largely unknown, however, is the rest of his own philosophy.

When people think of this Russian-born thinker, who became a French citizen in 1937, they generally remember only the “mask of Hegel” and one provocative thesis: “the end of history.” This naturally leads us to ask whether he understood the German philosopher correctly. Is his interpretation reliable?
But once those questions guide us, we set off down a path that takes us away from Kojève’s thought and, quite properly, toward Hegel’s.
Kojève himself cared very little about these questions or the criticisms they produced.
“The question of whether Hegel really says what I make him say is simply childish,” he remarks in the margin of a critical article.
In the long run, however, this attitude worked against the reception of Kojève’s own philosophy.

We still inherit this unstable situation today. On the one hand, we are fascinated by the power of his ideas. On the other, we are frustrated that they appear only in the course of a commentary—and an unfaithful commentary at that—which blurs the philosophy we are trying to understand, whether Kojève’s or Hegel’s.

After all, if the only substantial work published during Kojève’s lifetime was an Introduction to the Reading of Hegel, is it not reasonable for a reader of a “commentary” to expect access to Hegelian philosophy? And conversely, if we discover that the commentator is straying too far from his supposed master, is it not natural to abandon the commentator?
But did Kojève even want to publish the Introduction to the Reading of Hegel himself?

There are good reasons to doubt it. What became the book was largely made up of lecture notes taken by the writer Raymond Queneau—notes that were sometimes seriously incomplete and sometimes incorrect.

When one considers this, it is remarkable that some eighty years later an incomplete, unfaithful, and sometimes faulty course on Hegel should still enjoy such enormous popularity, not only in France but around the world.
The reason is that every reader senses that something else is happening in those pages.
Perhaps, as Kojève himself explained shortly before the Introduction to the Reading of Hegel appeared—and as the present book now confirms—it was a matter of “propaganda.”
That is to say, above all, it was a matter of struggle: a struggle carried out partly on the terrain of philosophy, with the aim of taking part in shaping the future of human history.

We can therefore say that, for the time being, every interpretation of Hegel, if it is more than mere chatter, is nothing but a program of struggle and work—one such “program” being called Marxism. This means that the work of an interpreter of Hegel has the significance of a work of political propaganda. M. Niel is therefore quite right to conclude that “Hegelianism has more than a purely literary interest.” For it may indeed be that the future of the world—and therefore the meaning of the present and the significance of the past—depends in the final analysis on how Hegel’s writings are interpreted today.
If the “future of the world” was still undecided, then Kojève’s undertaking was indeed a serious one, and his philosophy had to be equal to the scale of that claim.
But could it be, if it remained only a course on Hegel—or even merely someone else’s notes from such a course? Could the “future of the world” really rest on so little? Was that serious?
Edmond Ortigues, Kojève’s friend, reports a striking remark on this point. Kojève is said to have told him:
“Remember that I did not publish the Introduction to Hegel’s Phenomenology myself. It was published by a humorist, Raymond Queneau. That point is very important to me.”

Until now, then, Kojève left us in an unstable position. We had an introduction to Hegel that was also an introduction to his own philosophy; the immense seriousness of the “future of the world”; and yet a published “reading” assembled by a “humorist.”
With the publication of the present book, we now know that Kojève took his work of “propaganda” very seriously indeed.
And at the time, the public he really had in mind was essentially in Moscow.
Sophia and the Horizon of Russian Thought
As early as 1936, in a letter to Father Fessard, Kojève clearly placed himself within the intellectual world of Russia. In doing so, he also explained how he understood philosophy:

By examining your conscience, you rejoin the Catholic Church, and the publication of your book proves that it is also this Church that speaks through you. Your reader therefore encounters a collective consciousness, a collective force, a historical force conscious of itself. The very fact of publication therefore removes from your book the indecency and pretension necessarily involved in a strictly personal examination of conscience—a metaphysical “journal,” a “Reisetagebuch eines Philosopher”—which can be justified only by the artistic perfection of its form or by its absolute truth. In my own case, since I lack the necessary talent, artistic perfection is out of the question. And unfortunately, what I can communicate are not yet truths, but only examinations of conscience. In my case, publication would therefore be unjustified. It could have been justified, and I might have found myself in a situation analogous to yours, if my response could be published in Moscow.

What Kojève had hoped for in 1936, he began to put into practice between 1940 and 1941: to publish a book in Russia in which he could speak in his own name without this being “indecent”—which ultimately meant speaking on the scale of an entire people confronting universal history.
That imposing work is now before us.

Kojève, however, completed only a long introduction, which forms the first volume of our edition. And, as if to make his connection to the Russian intellectual world unmistakable, he gave this introduction a title whose significance would have been obvious to anyone familiar with Russian philosophy:
Kojève knew perfectly well where that title came from.

At the beginning of a 1932 seminar on “Russian religious philosophy,” devoted more specifically to Vladimir Soloviev, the subject of his doctoral thesis, Kojève made a passing remark that takes on a very different importance in light of the present text:

Later we will have to deal at length with the idea of Sophia—the Wisdom of God—which is the central idea of Soloviev’s philosophy, and of Russian religious philosophy in general. For the moment, I will say only that Sophia was not an abstract entity for Soloviev.
Kojève did indeed deal with Sophia at length—so much so that he eventually gave the name to what appears to be his opus magnum.

In doing so, he also puts his earlier lectures, whether on Hegel or on Russian religious philosophy, back into their proper place: they were preliminary stages leading toward this much larger undertaking.

In the Russian philosophical tradition to which Kojève belongs, Sophia was not an “abstract entity,” as he himself emphasizes. Sophia was humanity made whole: humanity united into a single body and ideally completed at the end of history in wisdom—that is, in perfect self-knowledge.
The difference is that the religious philosophers Kojève criticized called this final state the “Kingdom of God on Earth,” whereas Kojève, in this manuscript, calls it communism.

Communism is the moment when individuals are supposed to free themselves from the constraints of the collective while at the same time receiving universal recognition for their own individual self-creation. It is the moment when they free themselves from the species Homo sapiens, from nations, and from classes.
To use a proverbial formula especially common in Russian thought, it is the moment when, in the eyes of the Universal, there will no longer be Jew or Greek, man or woman.
So what, in the end, are we dealing with in this text?

A monumental panorama in which humanity emerges from animal life and reaches a condition resembling divinity through the Russian Revolution, which plants in the world the seed of a USSR destined eventually to realize the old dream of a universal and homogeneous Empire: a world without borders and without classes, in which individuals would become something like mortal gods.
Because of the book’s size, we have divided it into two volumes.
The first, entitled Philosophy and Phenomenology, was intended to be only the “introduction” to a future System of “Absolute” Knowledge.
The second, entitled Essay in a Dialectical Introduction to Philosophy, and left unfinished, contains the beginning of the project itself.

We felt it essential to add a number of notes explaining the Russian context, which will often be unfamiliar to French readers. Other notes address translation problems where these raise philosophical issues.
We have also reproduced the most important of Kojève’s marginalia.
Our editorial notes appear at the end of the book, while Kojève’s own notes appear in the appendix.

French terms that appeared in the Russian original are printed here in italics followed by an asterisk. Where a word seemed to be missing from the manuscript, we have supplied it between angle brackets.

Although the title of this introductory volume—Sophia: Philosophy and Phenomenology—appears to have been settled, Kojève seems to have hesitated over the title of the complete work. We therefore reproduce opposite this page the title-page design he seems to have envisaged.
